sections.title: Section 1 — Sports centre membership enquiry
sections.transcript:
RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help?

CALLER: Hello, I'd like some information about joining the centre. My name's Daniel Brooks.

RECEPTIONIST: Certainly. Could you spell your surname for me?

CALLER: Yes, it's B-R-O-O-K-S.

RECEPTIONIST: Thank you, Mr Brooks. And what's the best phone number for you?

CALLER: It's 0784 229 5163.

RECEPTIONIST: 0784 229 5163. Got it. Now, which activities are you interested in?

CALLER: Well, I mainly want to play badminton. I used to play at university.

RECEPTIONIST: We have four badminton courts. Which evening would suit you best?

CALLER: Thursday, I think. That's the only evening I'm free.

RECEPTIONIST: Thursday's fine — the courts are usually quieter then. Are you in full-time education at the moment?

CALLER: Yes, I'm doing a master's degree.

RECEPTIONIST: In that case you'd be eligible for a student membership. That's thirty-two pounds a month, and there's a one-off joining fee of fifteen pounds.

CALLER: That sounds reasonable. What about the swimming pool?

RECEPTIONIST: The pool opens at half past six in the morning and closes at ten at night. You'll need a one-pound coin for the lockers, by the way.

CALLER: And is there parking?

RECEPTIONIST: Yes, but it's only free after six in the evening. Before that you pay at the machine.

CALLER: Understood. One more thing — do new members get anything?

RECEPTIONIST: Yes, everyone gets a free induction session with one of our instructors, so you can find your way around the equipment.

CALLER: That's great. I'll come in on Saturday to sign up.

RECEPTIONIST: Perfect. See you then.

sections.title: Section 2 — Welcome talk at an eco park
sections.transcript:
GUIDE: Hello everyone, and welcome to Riverside Eco Park. I'm Maya, one of the volunteer guides, and I'll give you a short introduction before you explore.

The park opened twelve years ago on the site of an old water-treatment works, and it's now home to more than four hundred species of plants and animals. This year we've added something new: a butterfly garden next to the main lake. It's already attracting several species that we haven't seen here before.

If you'd like to join one of our guided walks, they leave from the main entrance every hour, on the hour. The walks take about ninety minutes and cover roughly two kilometres. I'd strongly recommend bringing walking shoes — some of the paths are uneven, especially after rain — and a waterproof jacket, because the weather here changes quickly.

The café near the car park serves hot food until four o'clock, but I should mention that it's closed on Mondays. The children's play area is right next to the café, so parents can keep an eye on the kids while they have a coffee.

If you're interested in plants, the rare orchid is flowering at the moment in the wetland area, which is the wet ground beyond the second bridge. Please stay on the boardwalk there — the soil is fragile.

A word about bikes: you're welcome to cycle on the main track, but bicycles aren't allowed on the north path, because it's narrow and shared with walkers.

If I could ask one favour: our biggest problem at the moment is litter. The bins are emptied every morning, but on busy weekends they fill up quickly, so please take your rubbish home with you.

Finally, if you'd like to help look after the park, we have a volunteers' group. They meet on the first Saturday of each month at nine o'clock by the tool shed. No experience is needed — just bring gloves.

Right, does anyone have any questions before we set off?

sections.title: Section 3 — Students discussing a research project
sections.transcript:
TUTOR: Come in, both of you. So, how's the project going?

ANNA: It's going well, I think. We've finished the reading and we're ready to start collecting data.

TUTOR: Remind me what the focus is.

ANNA: We're looking at the effect of city noise on the songs of small birds — specifically whether birds in busy areas sing at a higher pitch to be heard over traffic.

TUTOR: That's a nice question. What's your plan for the data?

TOM: We're going to use smartphones to record birdsong. They're not as good as professional recorders, but we can use a lot of them, so we can cover more sites.

TUTOR: How many sites?

TOM: Six, to begin with — three near main roads and three in quieter parks.

TUTOR: Good. And when will you record?

ANNA: At dawn, when the birds are most active. We'll do five mornings at each site.

TUTOR: That's sensible. Have you thought about permission? You'll need a permit from the council to record in the parks.

TOM: We didn't know that. We'll apply this week.

TUTOR: Do it early — it can take a while. One thing I'd suggest is that you write the literature review first, before the data collection. It'll help you sharpen the question, and you'll need it for the ethics form anyway.

ANNA: That makes sense. Is there anything you'd recommend reading?

TUTOR: There's a good book by Helen Smith on urban birdsong. I'll email you the reference.

TOM: Thanks. And how long should the final presentation be?

TUTOR: Twelve minutes, plus five minutes for questions. And remember, the project deadline is the end of the month — so you've got about three weeks.

ANNA: We'll make it work. Thanks for your time.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture on the history of the bicycle
sections.transcript:
LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at the history of a machine most of us take for granted: the bicycle.

The story begins in 1817, when a German baron called Karl von Drais built a wooden machine with two wheels in line, a seat, and a handlebar. It had no pedals at all. The rider sat on it and pushed his feet against the ground to move forward, a bit like running while sitting down. It was slow, but it was the first two-wheeled vehicle that balanced on its own.

In the 1860s, a French design attached pedals directly to the front wheel. This was faster, but the solid wooden wheels and the lack of any suspension made it extremely uncomfortable on cobbled streets. It earned a memorable nickname: the boneshaker.

By the 1870s, designers had realised that a larger front wheel meant more distance per turn of the pedals. The result was the penny-farthing, with a huge front wheel and a tiny rear one. It was fast, but it was also dangerous: the rider sat high up, and a small stone in the road could throw him over the handlebars.

The modern shape of the bicycle arrived in 1885 with John Kemp Starley's Rover. It had two wheels of equal size, a chain driving the rear wheel, and a frame that kept the rider low and stable. This "safety bicycle" is essentially the machine we ride today.

The ride became far more comfortable in 1888, when John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet, patented the pneumatic tyre — a rubber tyre filled with air instead of solid rubber. Combined with the safety frame, this made cycling smooth enough for ordinary people, including women in long skirts.

The social effects were enormous. Cycling gave women a degree of freedom that had been difficult to achieve, and it changed the design of women's clothing: long skirts were replaced by shorter ones and, eventually, by trousers. Some historians argue that the bicycle did more for women's mobility than any other invention of the period.

The 1890s saw a bicycle boom, with hundreds of manufacturers and a craze for cycling in Europe and North America. Prices fell, and the machine moved from a rich person's toy to everyday transport.

Today, the bicycle is again being taken seriously as a solution to urban problems. In the Netherlands and Denmark, cities have invested heavily in infrastructure for cyclists, and cycling is often described as one of the most efficient forms of transport ever invented: it uses no fuel, takes up little space, and keeps the rider fit. Not bad for a wooden machine from 1817.

Now, before I take questions, let me mention the reading for next week...
